title: Hi Sēf, what's new?
goal: Greet a friend the Emirati way, answer 'what's new?', and ask where someone is.
grammar: Independent pronouns: ana, inta, huwa; no word for 'is'
tip: Gulf Arabic has no 'is': huwa fi l-bēt = he (is) at home. So far: ana (I), inta (you, to a man), inti (you, to a woman), and now huwa (he). On a verb, -ah means 'him, it': nshūfah = we'll see him. Emiratis ask shḥālak?; your shlōnak? is just as good.
dialogue: هلا بك. بخير، الله يسلمك. وانت؟
hala bik. b-khēr, allāh ysallmak. w inta?
Hi. Fine, God keep you. And you?
هَلَا بِكْ. بْخَيْرْ، اللّٰهْ يْسَلّْمَكْ. وْاِنْتَ؟
ما شي. وين أحمد؟ هو في الجامعة؟
ma shay. wēn Aḥmad? huwa fi l-jāmʿa?
Not much. Where's Ahmed? Is he at the university?
مَا شَيْ. وَيْنْ أَحْمَدْ؟ هُوَ فِي الْجَامْعَة؟
Really? OK, we'll see him later.
items: to a woman: shḥālich (شحالج); shlōnak, which you know, is just as good
hi to you too; welcome (to a man)
to a woman: hala bich (هلا بج); replies to hala, and a host also opens with it to a guest
the usual answer: b-khēr, allāh ysallmak
a fixed reply: here ma goes before a noun
without the question mark it means 'honestly, I swear'
of a person: kind, nice (rayyāl ṭayyib)

title: Good morning, Maryam
goal: Greet a woman colleague, ask how she is with the -ich form, and ask about another colleague.
grammar: Pronoun hiya (she); -ich and -a when talking to a woman; no copula
tip: Speaking to a woman, words change: shḥālak → shḥālich (-ich = your), mashkūr → mashkūra (-a agrees with her). hiya = she, again with no 'is': hiya fi ijtimāʿ = she's in a meeting. hē is the Emirati 'yes'; your ī is fine too.
culture: Handshakes between men and women vary. Many Emirati women don't shake hands with men, so let a woman offer her hand first; if she doesn't, a smile and the greeting are enough, and some men touch their chest. Men usually shake hands with every man present.
dialogue: b-khēr, allāh ysallmak. w inta shakhbārak?
Fine, God keep you. And how are things with you?
زين الحمد لله. وسارة؟ هي في المكتب؟
zēn il-ḥamdu lillāh. w Sāra? hiya fi l-maktab?
Good, thank God. And Sara? Is she in the office?
زَيْنْ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهْ. وْسَارَة؟ هِيَ فِي الْمَكْتَبْ؟
هيه، بس هي في اجتماع الحين
hē, bas hiya fi ijtimāʿ il-ḥīn
Yes, but she's in a meeting now.
هَيْه، بَسْ هِيَ فِي اِجْتِمَاعْ الْحِينْ
items: to a man: shḥālak; shlōnich works too
to a woman: shakhbārich (شخبارج); reply: zēn il-ḥamdu lillāh
Kuwait: ēh (إيه); your ī (إي) is fine everywhere

title: We're students here
goal: Greet two students at the university, say who 'we' are, and ask a group questions.
grammar: Pronouns: niḥin (we) and intu (you, to a group)
tip: niḥin = we, intu = you (to a group), still with no 'is': niḥin ṭullāb = we're students. A verb to a group ends in -ūn: intu tidrisūn = you (all) study. as-salāmu ʿalaykum already greets everyone present.
dialogue: And upon you peace. Hi there.
hē, niḥin ṭullāb handasa. w inta?
Yes, we're engineering students. And you?
Me too. Are you from Dubai?
لا، نحن من العين، بس ندرس هني
la, niḥin min il-ʿĒn, bas nidris hni
No, we're from Al Ain, but we study here.
لَا، نِحِنْ مِنْ الْعَيْنْ، بَسْ نِدْرِسْ هْنِي
items: hi to you too (to a man)
to a woman: hala fīch (هلا فيج); to a group: hala fīkum (هلا فيكم); replies to hala; same as hala bik (هلا بك)
to one man: inta; to one woman: inti
to one man: tidris; to one woman: tidrisīn

title: Welcome! The guys are in the majlis
goal: Arrive at Sēf's house, answer a warm welcome, and pass greetings on to someone who isn't there.
grammar: Pronoun hum (they); the full set ana, inta, inti, huwa, hiya, niḥin, intu, hum
tip: hum = they, for men, women or a mix: hum fi l-majlis = they're in the majlis. The full set: ana, inta, inti, huwa, hiya, niḥin, intu, hum. ysallim ʿalēk = he says hi to you; for 'she', tsallim ʿalēk.
culture: When you walk into a majlis, say as-salāmu ʿalaykum to the whole room. The men there usually stand, and the newcomer goes round shaking hands, often starting from the right or with the oldest man.
dialogue: Welcome, welcome! Great to see you.
بخير، الله يسلمك. تفضل، الشباب في المجلس
b-khēr, allāh ysallmak. tfaẓẓal, ish-shabāb fi l-majlis
Fine, God keep you. Come in, the guys are in the majlis.
بْخَيْرْ، اللّٰهْ يْسَلّْمَكْ. تْفَضَّلْ، الشَّبَابْ فِي الْمَجْلِسْ
Who are they? Ahmed and Hamad?
هيه، هم كلهم هني. وخالد يسلم عليك
hē, hum killhum hni. w Khālid ysallim ʿalēk
Yes, they're all here. And Khalid says hi.
هَيْه، هُمْ كِلّْهُمْ هْنِي. وْخَالِدْ يْسَلِّمْ عَلَيْكْ
God keep him. Say hi to him (from me).
items: the majlis (the room where guests sit)
for men, women or a mix
(he) says hi to you (to a man)
to a woman: ysallim ʿalēch; she says hi: tsallim ʿalēk
God keep him (reply when he sends greetings)
say hi to him (from me) (to a man)
to a woman: sallmi ʿalēh; for her: sallim ʿalēha

title: Meeting Sēf's mum
goal: At Sēf's home, with Sēf there, greet his mother respectfully and answer her questions about your family with 'my' and 'your'.
tip: Add an ending to a noun for 'my' and 'your': ahal → ahli (my family), ahlak (your family, to a man), ahlich (to a woman). After a vowel, 'my' is -y: ubū → ubūy (my dad). walad (son) shortens: wildi (my son), wildich (your son, to a woman).
dialogue: God bless you. How are you?
بخير الحمد لله. وأهلك؟ عساهم بخير؟
b-khēr il-ḥamdu lillāh. w ahlak? ʿasāhum b-khēr?
Fine, thank God. And your family? I hope they're well?
بْخَيْرْ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهْ. وْأَهْلَكْ؟ عَسَاهُمْ بْخَيْرْ؟
الحمد لله بخير. أمي وأبوي في لندن
il-ḥamdu lillāh b-khēr. ummi w ubūy fi Landan
Fine, thank God. My mum and dad are in London.
الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهْ بْخَيْرْ. أُمِّي وْأُبُويْ فِي لَنْدَنْ
الله يحفظهم. وانت ويا ولدي في الجامعة؟
allāh yiḥfaẓhum. w inta wiyya wildi fi l-jāmʿa?
God protect them. And you're at the university with my son?
اللّٰهْ يِحْفَظْهُمْ. وْاِنْتَ وِيَّا وِلْدِي فِي الْجَامْعَة؟
هيه، في نفس الجامعة. سيف ربيعي
hē, fi nafs il-jāmʿa. Sēf rbīʿi
Yes, at the same university. Sēf's my friend.
هَيْه، فِي نَفْسْ الْجَامْعَة. سَيْفْ رْبِيعِي
items: your family: ahlak (to a man), ahlich (to a woman)
I hope they're well? (asking after family)
about one man: ʿasāh b-khēr?; you know ʿasāk b-khēr
said when someone mentions their family
with me: wiyyāy; with you: wiyyāk (to a man), wiyyāch (to a woman)
your son: wildak (to a man), wildich (to a woman)
fi nafs il-jāmʿa = at the same university
a woman says of her female friend: rbīʿti (ربيعتي; from a man it can sound like ‘my girlfriend’); my group of friends: rabʿi (ربعي)

title: Brothers and sisters
goal: Ask Maryam about her brothers and sisters and talk about yours.
grammar: Possessive endings -ak, -ich, -ha; family plurals learned as words
tip: Family plurals are learned as words: akh (brother) → ikhwān, ukhut (sister) → khawāt. Endings go on as usual: ikhwāni (my brothers), khawātich (your sisters, to a woman), rayyilha (her husband). ʿindich = you have (to a woman).
dialogue: hē, akh wāḥid bas. w inta?
Yes, just one brother. And you?
عندي ثلاث إخوان وأخت. إخواني في لندن
ʿindi thalāth ikhwān w ukhut. ikhwāni fi Landan
I have three brothers and a sister. My brothers are in London.
عِنْدِي ثَلَاثْ إِخْوَانْ وْأُخُتْ. إِخْوَانِي فِي لَنْدَنْ
ويا ريلها وعيالها في لندن. وانتي، عندج خوات؟
wiyya rayyilha w ʿyālha fi Landan. w inti, ʿindich khawāt?
With her husband and kids in London. And you, do you have sisters?
وِيَّا رَيِّلْهَا وْعْيَالْهَا فِي لَنْدَنْ. وْاِنْتِي، عِنْدِجْ خَوَاتْ؟
أخت وحدة. هي متزوجة، وريلها من الشارقة
ukhut waḥda. hiya mitzawwja, w rayyilha min ish-Shārja
One sister. She's married, and her husband is from Sharjah.
أُخُتْ وَحْدَة. هِيَ مِتْزَوّْجَة، وْرَيِّلْهَا مِنْ الشَّارْقَة
items: your brother: akhūk (to a man), akhūch (to a woman)
your sister: ukhtak (to a man), ukhtich (to a woman)
waḥda is wāḥid with feminine words
a woman: mitzawwja (متزوجة); UAE also: miʿarris (معرس)
lit. 'her man'; my husband (a woman says): rayyli

title: Family photos
goal: Look at Sēf's family photos, ask who's who, and praise the children the Gulf way.
grammar: Endings -ah (his) and -ha (her); ة becomes t before an ending or a noun
tip: -ah = his, -ha = her: bintah (his daughter), bint-ha (her daughter). A word ending in -a takes t before an ending or a following noun: ṣūra → ṣūrti (my photo), ṣūrat ahli (a photo of my family). wild ukhti = my sister's son.
culture: Praise a child, a house or a new car with mā shāʼ allāh. Praise without it can sound like envy (the evil eye), so Gulf speakers add it almost automatically, and often add a blessing for a child: allāh ykhallīh, allāh ykhallīha.
dialogue: This is a photo of my family.
This is my brother, and this is his daughter.
God bless her. What's her name?
اسمها حصة. وهذا ولد أختي، عمره سنتين
ismha Ḥiṣṣa. w hādha wild ukhti, ʿumrah santēn
Her name's Hessa. And this is my sister's son, he's two.
اِسْمْهَا حِصَّة. وْهٰذَا وِلْدْ أُخْتِي، عُمْرَهْ سَنْتَيْنْ
items: my photo: ṣūrti; a photo of my family: ṣūrat ahli
for a woman or girl: minu hādhi?
his daughter: bintah; her daughter: bint-ha
God bless her (said of a child)
of a boy: allāh ykhallīh; of them: allāh ykhallīhum
walad (boy, son) becomes wild before a noun
ʿumrah santēn = he's two; her age: ʿumrha
one year: sana; three years: thalāth sinīn (you've also seen thalāth sanawāt)
my kids: ʿyāli; UAE also: yahhāl (يهال)

title: Whose is this?
goal: Ask whose things are after a lecture and say what's yours with ḥagg.
grammar: ḥagg- 'belonging to': ḥaggi, ḥaggak, ḥaggah, ḥagg minu? (Kuwait: māl-)
tip: ḥagg + ending = mine, yours, his: ḥaggi, ḥaggak (to a man), ḥaggich (to a woman), ḥaggah, ḥagg-ha. Before a name: ḥagg Aḥmad = Ahmed's. 'Whose?' = ḥagg minu? Kuwaitis also say māl: māli, mālak. But ʿind- takes ma: mub ḥaggi (not mine), ma ʿindi (I don't have).
dialogue: مب حقي، ما عندي شنطة. حق أحمد؟
mub ḥaggi, ma ʿindi shanṭa. ḥagg Aḥmad?
Not mine, I don't have a bag. Ahmed's?
مُبْ حَقِّي، مَا عِنْدِي شَنْطَة. حَقّْ أَحْمَدْ؟
لا، أحمد في البيت اليوم. مب حقه
la, Aḥmad fi l-bēt il-yōm. mub ḥaggah
No, Ahmed's at home today. It isn't his.
لَا، أَحْمَدْ فِي الْبَيْتْ الْيَوْمْ. مُبْ حَقَّهْ
OK, and the book? Is it yours?
العفو. الشنطة حق فاطمة! هذا اسمها
il-ʿafu. ish-shanṭa ḥagg Fāṭma! hādha ismha
You're welcome. The bag is Fatma's! Here's her name.
الْعَفُو. الشَّنْطَة حَقّْ فَاطْمَة! هٰذَا اِسْمْهَا
items: ḥagg Aḥmad = Ahmed's; Kuwait also: māl (مال)
hādha ḥagg minu? = whose is this?
before ʿind- use ma, not mub: ma ʿindi shanṭa; you don't have: ma ʿindak (to a man), ma ʿindich (to a woman)

title: Sēf's dad's car
goal: Talk about whose car and whose house it is, using two nouns together.
grammar: The construct: noun + owner for 'X of Y' (bēt ubūy, sayyārat ubūy)
tip: Put the owner straight after the thing, with no word for 'of': bēt yaddi = my grandad's house. A word ending in -a takes -at: sayyāra → sayyārat ubūy (my dad's car). Only the second noun takes il- or an ending.
dialogue: ويا ولد عمي اليوم. هو ريّال طيب
wiyya wild ʿammi l-yōm. huwa rayyāl ṭayyib
My cousin has it today. He's a good guy.
وِيَّا وِلْدْ عَمِّي الْيَوْمْ. هُوَ رَيَّالْ طَيِّبْ
OK, and where are we going?
بيت يدي ويدتي. كل الأهل هناك
bēt yaddi w yaddti. kill il-ahal hnāk
To my grandparents' house. The whole family's there.
بَيْتْ يَدِّي وْيَدّْتِي. كِلّْ الْأَهَلْ هْنَاكْ
items: a car: sayyāra (سيارة); your car: sayyārtak (to a man)
a girl cousin: bint ʿammi (بنت عمي)
you'll see written ريال, which is also the riyal coin
yaddi = my grandfather; you'll see written جدي
one man: rāyiḥ; one woman: rāyḥa

title: Asking after the family
goal: Visit Sēf's family with Sēf: answer his mother's welcome, ask after her, and show her where your family lives.
tip: -na = our, -kum = your (to a group or a whole family), -hum = their: bētna (our house), bētkum (your house), ʿyālhum (their kids). After t, d, g, k or s, a hyphen goes before -ha and -hum, so you don't read th, dh, gh, kh or sh: bēt-hum, ḥagg-ha.
culture: Ask after a family as a whole: shḥāl il-ahal? (how's the family?) or ʿasāhum b-khēr? Don't ask a man about his wife by name; ask after 'the family' or 'the house' instead.
dialogue: حياك الله يا ولدي. شحال الأهل؟
ḥayyāk allāh yā wildi. shḥāl il-ahal?
حَيَّاكْ اللّٰهْ يَا وِلْدِي. شْحَالْ الْأَهَلْ؟
الله يحييج يا خالتي. كلهم بخير. وانتي؟
allāh yḥayyīch yā khālti. killhum b-khēr. w inti?
God bless you, auntie. They're all well. And you?
اللّٰهْ يْحَيِّيجْ يَا خَالْتِي. كِلّْهُمْ بْخَيْرْ. وْاِنْتِي؟
الحمد لله. وين ساكنين؟ في لندن؟
il-ḥamdu lillāh. wēn sāknīn? fi Landan?
Fine, thank God. Where do they live? In London?
الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهْ. وَيْنْ سَاكْنِينْ؟ فِي لَنْدَنْ؟
Yes. Here, this is (a photo of) our house.
ما شاء الله، بيتكم حلو. وهذا منو؟
mā shāʼ allāh, bētkum ḥilu. w hādha minu?
Lovely, your house is nice. And who's this?
مَا شَاءْ اللّٰهْ، بَيْتْكُمْ حِلُو. وْهٰذَا مِنُو؟
That's my sister's husband, with their kids.
items: son, my boy (an older person to a young man)
an older person to a young woman: yā binti (يا بنتي)
the polite way to ask after someone's family
a man: sākin; a woman: sākna
here you are, please (to a woman)
to a man: tfaẓẓal (you know it)
your house (to a group or a family)
to one man: bētak; to one woman: bētich
rayyāl (man) becomes rayyil before a noun or ending
our kids: ʿyālna; your kids (to a group): ʿyālkum
auntie (respectful, to an older woman, e.g. a friend's mother)
to an older man: yā ʿammi (يا عمي)
